mission_3.rationale: I made two changes. The first was to increase the confirmation timeout from 18 seconds to 30 seconds. In the baseline clear_request trial, the participant hesitated before confirming, and my relayed “yes” arrived after the request had expired, producing an error. The participant was then unsure whether they had to ask again. A longer window should let a slower confirmation arrive before the request expires, so a short pause no longer causes a failure. The second change was to rewrite the listening message so it gives an example request, says to reply “yes” after the robot repeats it, and says that after a timeout nothing happened and they should type the request again. In the baseline no_response trial, the participant did not know what to do after the timeout, and in alternate_modality they typed a command without the expected syntax and nothing happened. Showing the expected input and the recovery step at the moment of listening removes the need to guess. In the retest, the participant said they liked that the listening message told them to enter the command again after an error or timeout.
mission_3.comparison: With the same participant (P-2305) and the same five scenarios, task success rose from 0.8 to 1.0 and intent comprehension rose from 0.8 to 1.0. Mean predictability rose from 3.6 to 5.0 and mean feedback clarity rose from 4.0 to 5.0. Listening clarity and recovery stayed at 1.0, and there were no safety stops in either session, so I found no regressions. Mean completion time fell from 40 seconds to 31 seconds. Most of that came from clear_request (20 s to 10 s) and alternate_modality (90 s to 60 s). The correction trial was 5 seconds faster even though nothing was changed for that scenario, which suggests the participant, not the redesign, caused that gain. The no_response and ambiguous_request times were unchanged. These results should be read cautiously. The participant saw the same five scenarios in the same order, so learning effects are likely. In fact, I noted that they moved through the first scenario quickly because they knew what to expect. I was still the facilitator, and the ratings are all 5s from one person, so these results cannot show that the redesign is generally more usable. One problem remains. The alternate_modality task succeeded in the retest, but the participant said syntax was still an issue, so the root cause was only softened.
mission_3.next_iteration: For the next iteration, the main target is the text-command syntax problem that remained in alternate_modality. The accessibility improvement would be to accept plain-language text input, or at least to show a syntax example in the text-command prompt. This would help people who cannot or prefer not to use the primary command method, and it would remove the dependency on knowing a command format. I would also add a new failure-recovery test, a malformed command scenario. The participant types a command the system cannot parse, and I observe whether the display tells them what went wrong and how to fix it, whether they recover without facilitator help, and how long it takes. This tests a failure the current five scenarios do not cover. It would also be better to run the next test with a new participant and a different scenario order, so learning and order effects are separated from the effect of the design.
